title: Chapter VII
focus: the Plaza and the death car

teacherSummary.text: On the hottest day of summer Gatsby and Nick lunch with the Buchanans; Tom realizes Daisy loves Gatsby. They drive to the city, Tom in Gatsby's yellow car. At the Plaza, Tom exposes Gatsby's bootlegging; Daisy says she loved both. Driving home in Gatsby's car, Daisy hits Myrtle, who runs into the road, killing her. Gatsby waits outside the Buchanans' house; Nick sees Tom and Daisy conspiring.

context.history: The Plaza Hotel on Fifth Avenue was a landmark of luxury. Tom's charge that Gatsby and Wolfshiem 'bought up a lot of side-street drug-stores' reflects a real Prohibition practice: pharmacies could sell alcohol on prescription and served as fronts for bootlegging. Cars were new and lightly regulated; traffic deaths rose sharply in the 1920s.

significance: The climax: in one afternoon Gatsby's dream is exposed as resting on crime and on a past he cannot erase, and the car, the novel's symbol of status and danger, becomes a weapon. Responsibility for Myrtle's death begins to be shifted from the careless to the dreamer.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this novel is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Chapter VII,” how does Fitzgerald show the Plaza and the death car? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the setting you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter VII, how does Fitzgerald develop the idea of the Plaza and the death car? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the setting in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter VII develops the idea of the Plaza and the death car. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of setting and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter VII (where it begins, turns and ends) and its setting shape the reader's understanding of the Plaza and the death car. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter VII suggests about the Plaza and the death car. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's setting and characterization), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how F. Scott Fitzgerald uses setting in Chapter VII to complicate the reader's understanding of the Plaza and the death car. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter VII within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of the Plaza and the death car responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter VII alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of the Plaza and the death car follows or bends those conventions, using the setting as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter VII and its treatment of the Plaza and the death car. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's setting and characterization, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter VII as evidence for a larger claim about the Plaza and the death car in The Great Gatsby. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter VII as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of the Plaza and the death car. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on The Great Gatsby.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the chapter to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.
